Epithet

EP-uh-thet -- from Greek epi- ('upon, in addition') + tithenai ('to place, put'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Epithet is descriptive nickname or label.

Journalists began attaching the epithet 'the Iron Duke' to the general after his fourth consecutive victory.

Worked Example

After a pitcher throws a perfect game, sportswriters start calling him 'Iceman' in every headline for the rest of the season.

That descriptive nickname, attached to a name because it captures something notable about the person, is exactly what an epithet is.

How Epithet Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

moniker

moniker: an informal name or nickname

sobriquet

sobriquet: a nickname, often affectionately or humorously given

Antonyms

anonymity

anonymity: the state of being unknown or unnamed

obscurity

obscurity: the state of being unknown or forgotten

How Strong Is It? — moniker → epithet → sobriquet

moniker vs. epithet

moniker vs. epithet: Moniker is the most casual of the two -- almost any nickname, however plain, can be a moniker, while an epithet usually captures something specific and notable about the person or thing it describes.

sobriquet vs. epithet

sobriquet vs. epithet: Sobriquet is close in formality to epithet, and the two are nearly interchangeable, though sobriquet is slightly more associated with playful or affectionate nicknames, while epithet leans toward respectful or historical titles.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — epi-

prefix — epi-: upon, in addition (Greek)

root — -thet-

root — -thet-: to place, put (Greek (tithenai))

Put it together

Put it together: Epithet comes from Greek epi- ('upon, in addition') plus tithenai ('to place, put') -- so an epithet is literally something 'placed upon' a name, a descriptive label attached to identify or characterize a person.

Word Choice

Epithet most often names a respectful or descriptive nickname, especially a historical one like 'Alexander the Great,' though informally the word is sometimes used for an insulting label instead -- context usually makes the tone clear.
